| [![arXiv](https://img.shields.io/badge/arXiv-2610.38589-b31b1b.svg)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38589) | **GRAVITY-RESOLVE: A comprehensive image reconstruction tool for Galactic Center observations with GRAVITY**  |
|| K. A. E. Dayem, et al. -- incl., <mark>W. Brandner</mark>, <mark>P. Garcia</mark>, <mark>L. Kreidberg</mark>, <mark>J. Sauter</mark> |
|*Appeared on*| *2026-10-30*|
|*Comments*| *Submitted to Astronomy & Astrophysics (A&A) on October 24, 2026*|
|**Abstract**|            We aim to improve and extend the imaging capabilities of the GRAVITY beam combiner instrument of ESOs VLTI with respect to reconstruction software in the Galactic Center. We revise and develop the image reconstruction code GRAVITY-RESOLVE $\text{G}^{\text{R}}$, which has been specifically developed to reconstruct stars in the Galactic Center with GRAVITY. The main objectives are to increase the limiting magnitude in GRAVITY images, reduce its computational runtime, and allow for a joint reconstruction of multiple, spatially separate datasets/pointings on sky. We apply $\text{G}^{\text{R}}$ to recent GRAVITY data, featuring the implemented GRAVITY-faint mode as part of GRAVITY+, the upgrade of GRAVITY. We reconstruct visibility phases and amplitudes and present the first GRAVITY image reconstructed with $\text{G}^{\text{R}}$ from these quantities. We demonstrate NIR mosaicking with $\text{G}^{\text{R}}$ by jointly reconstructing nine separately acquired datasets of 2025 into a single image on a scale of $\simeq 3390\ \text{AU}\times 3390\ \text{AU}$, corresponding to $409.6\ \text{mas}\times 409.6\ \text{mas}$. With dedicated injection tests of point sources into GRAVITY data, we estimate the limiting magnitude to be $m_{\text{K}}\ \simeq\ 20.0$ within a radius of $25\ \text{mas}$ around the field center when reconstructing from closure phases and visibility amplitudes. We report on the discovery of two new faint stars in the Galactic Center: S303 and S304. Finally, we find a decrease in computational runtime by a factor of at least $\sim10$. With $\text{G}^{\text{R}}$, we demonstrate GRAVITYs capabilities for NIR imaging. We show that $\text{G}^{\text{R}}$ is a fast, precise, and deep image reconstruction tool for Galactic Center observations, enabling the discovery of even more faint stars.         |

| [![arXiv](https://img.shields.io/badge/arXiv-2610.38280-b31b1b.svg)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38280) | **Machine Learning Based Classification of Type 1 Active Galactic Nuclei**  |
|| <mark>J. Li</mark>, X.-L. Fan |
|*Appeared on*| *2026-10-30*|
|*Comments*| *14 Figures, 3 tables, accepted for publication in A&A*|
|**Abstract**|            Aims. We aim to provide a machine learning based method to distinguish type 1 quasars and type 1 Seyfert galaxies based on photometric data, which could be applied to large all-sky surveys. The method can also be used to obtain relatively complete samples of Seyfert galaxy candidates when broad-line AGNs have been selected. Results. The results of PCA show that quasars and Seyfert galaxies are partial distinguishable. The supervised classifier based on random forest (RF) achieves good performances for type 1 quasars with a F1 score of 0.967. The performance for classifying Seyfert galaxies is worse, with a F1 score of 0.791. Increasing the classification threshold can help to derive a sample of Seyfert galaxies with high purity. The classifier are then applied to the cross-matched sample with DESI DR1. When compared with the results of spectroscopic classification, quasars also show high precision and recall. For Seyfert galaxies identified by RF classifier, there are plenty of less luminous sources who are classified as quasars by spectroscopic method. If they are regarded as Seyfert galaxies, our classifier also performs well to predict Seyfert galaxies. Both the median SEDs and the fraction of Seyfert galaxies derived by our classifier are similar with those for the training sample, while the fraction of Seyfert galaxies for spectroscopic classification are lower at all redshift. These results indicate that our classifier can recover the features of Seyfert galaxies, at least those similar to the Seyfert galaxies in the training sample.         |

| [![arXiv](https://img.shields.io/badge/arXiv-2610.40045-b31b1b.svg)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40045) | **SDSS-V LVM: Mapping of plasma temperatures in the Lagoon Nebula reveals the origin of long-standing chemical abundance discrepancies**  |
|| A. Singh, et al. -- incl., <mark>K. Kreckel</mark> |
|*Appeared on*| *2026-10-30*|
|*Comments*| *Accepted to ApJ. 12 pages, 6 Figures*|
|**Abstract**|            Knowing the chemical composition of interstellar gas is essential for understanding the chemical evolution of galaxies. Ionized nebulae provide key laboratories for this purpose, where chemical abundances are commonly derived from emission lines of heavy ions such as doubly ionized oxygen, $O^{++}$. Abundances can be inferred either from collisionally excited lines (CELs) or from recombination lines (RLs). However, for more than 80 years, the former have yielded systematically lower abundances than the latter. We map this ''abundance discrepancy'' using the first spatially resolved integral field unit (IFU) observations of $O^{++}$ RLs and CELs across a Milky Way H II region: the Lagoon Nebula (a.k.a. M8). Modeling the data using a plasma temperature perturbation model, we present unequivocal evidence that electron temperature ($T_e$) fluctuations drive the abundance discrepancy in M8. We find a tight correlation between the abundance discrepancy and the difference between $T_e$ derived from the classical CEL method and a hybrid RL/CEL approach. We identify this Te discrepancy as an observational proxy for the amplitude of the thermal fluctuations, providing a new, direct way to quantify their effect on nebular abundances. The correlation constrains the mean electron temperature of the gas. Adopting this mean temperature reconciles CEL and RL abundances, effectively eliminating the abundance discrepancy.         |

| [![arXiv](https://img.shields.io/badge/arXiv-2610.38419-b31b1b.svg)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38419) | **The Ubiquity of White-Light Flares on the Sun**  |
|| S. Li, et al. -- incl., <mark>M. Zhang</mark> |
|*Appeared on*| *2026-10-30*|
|*Comments*| *Submitted. Comments are welcome!*|
|**Abstract**|            White-light flares (WLFs) have long been considered rare on the Sun, as most magnetic reconnections occur in the corona, making it difficult to transport sufficient energy downward to heat the very low layers for WL continuum emission. However, it is also argued that WL continuum emission is a common feature of all flares, and the rare detection of them is largely due to the limited sensitivity and resolution of telescopes. Recently, we developed a new method to identify WLFs, which exhibits extraordinary detection capability. Combined with SDO/HMI's over 15 years of continuous photospheric observations, it provides us an unprecedented opportunity to address the long-standing debate about WLF ubiquity. A total of 1951 flares (547 B-class, 1316 C-class, and 88 M-class) from 769 low-activity active regions (ARs; flare number $<$ 10) observed during January 2011 - May 2025 are investigated. Among these, 1012 are identified as WLFs, giving an overall occurrence rate of 51.9\%. The occurrence rates for B-, C-, and M-class flares are 36.9\%, 56.9\%, and 85.2\%, respectively, showing a clear increase with flare class. The occurrence rate is also highly correlated with the AR's sunspot number. For the first time, we find that WL continuum radiation is widely present even among B-class flares. Different WLFs contain varying numbers of WL kernels, which exhibit distinct properties, evolutionary behaviors and different relationships with GOES soft X-ray flux and its time derivative. These results strongly suggest that WLFs are a common phenomenon on the Sun.         |

| [![arXiv](https://img.shields.io/badge/arXiv-2610.39384-b31b1b.svg)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39384) | **The Disk Awakens: IXPE's Sequel Observation of GS 1354-64 Suggests Changing-Look Behavior in the Steep-Power-Law State**  |
|| S. Ravi, et al. -- incl., <mark>Y. Zhang</mark> |
|*Appeared on*| *2026-10-30*|
|*Comments*| *23 pages, 10 figures, Submitted to ApJ*|
|**Abstract**|            After decades of only failed transitions, the black hole X-ray binary GS 1354-64 has undergone a complete outburst again. We present its first X-ray polarimetric investigation in the fading steep-power-law (SPL) state, following an earlier intermediate-state IXPE campaign during the same outburst. The 2-8 keV emission has a polarization degree (PD) of 2.3 +/- 0.2% and polarization angle (PA) of 5 +/- 3 degrees. Compared with the intermediate state, where PD=3.9 +0.3/-0.2% and PA=-2 +/-2 degrees, the broadband PD is lower while the PA remains consistent. The intermediate-state type-C quasi-periodic oscillation state has also disappeared, marking a major reconfiguration of the accretion flow. Assuming a distance of 7 kpc, the observed the intensity drop from 2.5% to 1.6% of the Eddington luminosity over 10.2 days is punctuated by several broad hour-to-day-scale troughs, tracing two distinct tracks in hardness-intensity space. Simultaneous spectroscopy shows the troughs' spectra contains a cooler disk with smaller apparent normalization, while no change in the Compton component's photon index or normalization is required between tracks. The model-independent analysis identifies a steeper increase in PD with energy outside the troughs, yielding G_E=1.5 +/- 0.2%/keV, compared with G_E=0.7 +0.3/-0.5%/keV during the troughs. Their duration and spectropolarimetric morphology distinguish the troughs from traditional short absorption dips seen in X-ray binaries, providing a possible stellar-mass analog of the recurrent accretion changes that drive "changing-look" behavior in supermassive black hole systems.         |

| [![arXiv](https://img.shields.io/badge/arXiv-2610.40255-b31b1b.svg)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40255) | **A Candidate Binary Microlensing Event in the 2018 Gamma-Ray Flare of 3C 279**  |
|| Y. Yang, et al. -- incl., <mark>H. Zhang</mark> |
|*Appeared on*| *2026-10-30*|
|*Comments*| *12 pages, 7 figures*|
|**Abstract**|            The April 2018 gamma-ray flare of the flat-spectrum radio quasar 3C~279 exhibited sharp peaks within a broader outburst. Its rapid substructure was previously attributed to magnetic reconnection. Motivated by its distinctive temporal profile within our comparison sample of bright blazar flares and its resemblance to caustic-crossing features in optical microlensing events, we investigate a finite-source binary-microlensing interpretation. A jointly fitted model of binary-lens magnification, a smooth intrinsic flare, and Gaussian-process variability reproduces the principal double-peaked structure of the GeV light curve. The adopted local solution has a binary mass ratio of $q\simeq0.098$ and an Einstein timescale of $t_{\rm E}\simeq0.327$~d. The absolute lens mass and projected source radius depend on the lens distance and relative proper motion. The fitted geometry can correspond to a Galactic planetary-mass binary or an intervening stellar or substellar system, with different physical source sizes in each case. We present binary microlensing as a testable interpretation of this event, with the finite-source structure offering a potential probe of the compact GeV-emitting region.         |

| [![arXiv](https://img.shields.io/badge/arXiv-2610.40346-b31b1b.svg)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40346) | **Six New Eclipsing AM CVn Binaries from the Zwicky Transient Facility**  |
|| A. Householder, et al. -- incl., <mark>Y. Zhang</mark> |
|*Appeared on*| *2026-10-30*|
|*Comments*| *12 pages, 5 figures, 1 table. Submitted to ApJ*|
|**Abstract**|            We present the discovery of six new eclipsing AM CVn binaries, helium-accreting ultracompact systems in which a cool donor eclipses the accreting white dwarf. The systems were found in a GPU-accelerated Box Least Squares (BLS) search of Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) photometry and have orbital periods of 39.3 to 59.9 minutes. We obtained spectroscopy with the Low Resolution Imaging Spectrometer (LRIS) on the Keck I telescope for all six systems, and every spectrum shows helium emission with no detectable hydrogen, confirming their AM CVn classification. Our discoveries increase the number of deeply eclipsing AM CVn from 11 to 17 (i.e., systems in which the accreting white dwarf is both the dominant source of optical light and eclipsed by the donor). With high-speed photometric follow-up, these systems will provide the mass ratios, inclinations, and fractional radii of both components. They will also provide new tests of AM CVn formation models and stronger constraints on the long-term evolution of these sources.         |
